sentences.text: Behind the houses at Ferrel there is a wood of holm oak and in it there are the mounds, and the mounds are the largest thing about that village that visitors never notice.

There are four of them and the biggest is chest high and about three metres across and it is made of needle litter and it has been there, according to a man who did a survey in 1998, for at least a century.
It is a wood ant nest and there are perhaps a quarter of a million animals in it and it is entirely ordinary and there are ten thousand like it in Portugal.
Mariana has stood next to it a great many times.

In August it is loud — you can hear it from about four metres, a dry continuous crackle that is nothing but a quarter of a million small feet on dry needles — and it is warm, properly warm, several degrees above the air, which is a thing wood ant nests do and which has been measured and is not mysterious.
There is nothing about that mound that would make anybody look at it twice.
That is the point everybody in Ferrel makes when it comes up.
It is a completely ordinary nest of a completely ordinary species that any child in southern Europe can find in an afternoon.
The way you ask is this.
You open the window on the wood side of the house, the whole window, at dusk, and you leave it open all night, and you do not shut it and you do not go into that room.
That is all.
There is no phrase and no offering and nothing is left on the sill.
In the morning the house has stopped arguing.
That is the phrase.
Not *the argument is over* and not *you have made up*.
The house has stopped arguing, which is a claim about the house, and Mariana did not notice the grammar of it until she was about nineteen.
Mariana had known the mechanism since she was small and had never seen it done, because it is not done often.
Her grandmother reckoned three or four times a year across a village of a hundred and sixty people.

It is not a secret and it is not a ritual and there is no shame in it, and if you go past a house on the wood side at ten at night in April and the big window is open you look away, the way you would look away from a car with somebody sitting in it not driving.
Mariana saw an open window twice before she was twelve.
The first was the Estrela house in 2016 and she was seven and did not know what she was looking at.
The second was in 2019, in the summer, and she was ten and knew exactly what she was looking at and did not tell the person she was walking with, who was her friend Rita, whose house it was.
Rita has never mentioned it.
Mariana has never mentioned it.
They are still friends.
She asked her grandmother, at nine, what it cost.
Her grandmother said: "It costs the argument." Mariana said that was the point.
And her grandmother said, "Yes," in the particular way she said yes when a conversation had reached the edge of what she was going to say, and Mariana did not get any further with it for four years.
She tried again at eleven with a better question, which was whether her grandmother had ever done it.

Her grandmother said that she had, once, in 1981, and that she was not going to say what about, and that Mariana was to leave it, and that if she ever needed to know more than that she would find out for herself and would not enjoy it.
